query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In multi‐phase eutectic HEAs at elevated temperature, the accelerated coupled degradation is driven by the wear-induced breakup of the protective oxide/passive film at the heterogeneous phase boundaries. This film rupture exposes dissimilar phases with differing electrochemical potentials to the corrosive environment, triggering localized galvanic corrosion. The ensuing corrosion further degrades the microstructure, weakening the material and thereby increasing its susceptibility to mechanical wear in a mutually reinforcing cycle.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, equilibrated eutectic high‐entropy alloy with distinct multi‐phase microstructure and well‐defined phase boundaries and interfaces.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to cyclic wear-corrosion tests at an elevated temperature while maintaining matched conditions for wear-only and corrosion-only tests.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (e.g., ~800 K) environment in a corrosive medium (such as a saline solution) with controlled cyclic mechanical loading simulating sliding wear.
generation.structural_mediator: The phase boundaries and the associated passive/oxide film that forms on the heterogeneous interface between the different phases.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear disrupts and removes the stable passive film at the phase boundaries, exposing chemically heterogeneous and galvanically active interfaces. This then drives localized galvanic corrosion, which further undermines the mechanical integrity of the material, leading to accelerated degradation beyond simply additive effects of wear and corrosion acting independently.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (independent wear-only and corrosion-only conditions), the combined wear-corrosion condition will exhibit a substantially higher overall degradation rate. This will manifest as increased wear volume and higher corrosion current densities that exceed the sum of the individual modes, demonstrating a synergistic rather than an additive effect.
generation.baseline: Matched samples tested independently under wear-only and corrosion-only conditions at the same elevated temperature.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic coupling is expected to prevail under high-temperature conditions where passive film formation and its mechanical disruption coexist, and where the corrosive media (e.g., chloride-based solution) and mechanical load parameters are held constant to isolate the synergy between wear and corrosion.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative synergistic interaction is supported, the precise quantification of the acceleration in degradation (i.e., the exact increase in wear and corrosion rates) remains uncertain due to the complex interplay of microstructural factors and oxide film kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct cyclic tribo-corrosion tests on the HEA samples under three sets of conditions: (1) wear-only in an inert electrolyte, (2) corrosion-only without mechanical load, and (3) combined wear and corrosion under identical temperature and environmental settings. Compare the total degradation in terms of material loss, wear volume, and corrosion current densities.
measurements: Corrosion rate (e.g., via potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the degradation observed in the combined wear-corrosion tests is not significantly greater than the sum of the wear-only and corrosion-only degradations, then the hypothesis—that wear-induced passive film rupture at phase boundaries drives synergistic degradation—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeNiMn HEA coatings exhibit single-phase FCC structures, while the CoCrFeNiTi coating comprises FCC, Laves, and η phases, and the CoCrFeNiMo coating consists of FCC and σ phases. Among these, the CoCrFeNiMo coating demonstrates the highest hardness (~700 HV) and optimal wear resistance due to σ-phase strengthening, with oxidative wear identified as the dominant wear mechanism. However, the multiphase structures induce galvanic corrosion effects, resulting in comparatively inferior corrosion resistance for both CoCrFeNiMo and CoCrFeNiTi coatings.

This study systematically investigates the microstructure evolution, tribological properties, and corrosion mechanisms of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings fabricated via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding under variable laser power conditions. The key findings and implications are summarized as follows: The CoCrFeNiMo coatings exhibited a dual-phase structure comprising FCC and σ phases. At 2250 W, optimized energy density promoted homogeneous dispersion of Fe-Cr-rich σa and Fe-Mo-rich σb phases within the FCC matrix, forming a refined eutectic–hypereutectic hybrid microstructure. The hardness of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coatings increased with laser power, peaking at 738.3 HV0.2 at 2250 W. This improvement was attributed to solution strengthening and second-phase intensification. However, at 2000 W, the hardness decreased due to grain coarsening caused by the extended molten pool duration. At a laser power of 2250 W, the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating exhibited the lowest coefficient of friction (COF = 0.084) and excellent wear resistance. frame.system: A multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy in its as-cast, equilibrated eutectic microstructure with distinct phase boundaries and interfaces.
frame.goal: To identify a single, unified mechanistic explanation for the observed accelerated degradation when wear and corrosion occur simultaneously at elevated temperature, and to predict how this mechanism alters both the total degradation rate and the separate contributions of wear and corrosion compared to a baseline (e.g., tests in which the degradation modes act independently).
frame.limitation: The current lack of understanding of how the synergistic interaction between wear and corrosion at high temperature accelerates overall degradation relative to the sum of their individual effects.
constraints: The hypothesis must account for the interaction between wear and corrosion in a single mechanistic framework.
A controlled comparison must be specified (using a matched baseline that separately exposes the sample to wear-only and corrosion-only conditions).
Clear definition of boundary conditions and an explicit falsification criterion are required.
frame.regime: High-temperature conditions where both mechanical (wear) and chemical (corrosion) stresses are simultaneously active. Testing should involve controlled environments to isolate and combine these effects, such as cyclic wear-corrosion tests with calibrated potentials and mechanical loads.
prior_attempts: Previous studies have separately characterized wear and corrosion mechanisms in high-entropy alloys and assumed additive effects rather than true synergistic coupling.

Prior work using isolated degradation tests could not replicate the accelerated overall damage observed under simultaneous exposure, thus failing to capture the interfacial and microstructural factors that promote synergy.
